content.title: Revising Scientific Models Based on Evidence
content.overview: In the ACT Science section, you must be able to identify when a scientific model's predictions fail to match experimental data and determine how to update that model. This involves quantifying the gap between prediction and reality, identifying the specific variables causing the gap, and selecting the most efficient (minimal) revision to the model.
learning_objectives: Identify systematic deviations between a model's predictions and observed experimental data.
Link observed data deviations to specific experimental conditions or variables.
Select the most appropriate minimal revision to a model that accounts for new evidence.
Formulate new testable predictions based on a revised scientific model.

sections.title: Identifying the Need for Revision
sections.content: A scientific model is a representation used to explain or predict phenomena. A revision is triggered when observed data differ from the model's predictions beyond expected measurement noise. To identify a 'signal' for revision, look for a consistent pattern of deviation rather than a single outlier. You must quantify where the deviation starts (e.g., at a specific time or temperature) and the magnitude of the gap between the predicted value and the actual observation.

sections.title: Linking Deviations to Variables
sections.content: Once a deviation is identified, you must determine which variable is responsible. This is called 'condition linkage.' If a model predicts the same outcome for two groups, but the data shows they behave differently, the variable that distinguishes those groups (e.g., nutrient levels, pressure, or light exposure) must be incorporated into the revised model. The deviation should covary—change in tandem—with the specific experimental condition.

sections.title: The Principle of Minimal Revision
sections.content:
When updating a model, the ACT favors the 'minimal revision.' This means choosing the smallest change that explains the observed pattern without discarding the parts of the model that still work. Avoid 'over-correcting' by changing the entire model (e.g., switching from linear to exponential growth) if a simple adjustment to one variable's rate at a specific time suffices. A valid revision must also produce a new, testable prediction.

![A flowchart showing the steps to revise a scientific model: Identify Deviation, Link to Variable, Apply Minimal Revision, and State New Prediction.](https://img.justsolvely.com/followUpImage/770dbf69-28a8-42e8-b984-70dc47e8f866-1786506738437-266.webp)

worked_examples.question: A model predicts that all seedlings will grow at a constant rate of 2.0 cm/day regardless of nutrient levels. Data shows: Day 2: High Nutrient (4.1 cm), Low Nutrient (3.9 cm); Day 4: High (8.3 cm), Low (7.8 cm); Day 6: High (12.6 cm), Low (9.2 cm); Day 8: High (17.0 cm), Low (10.0 cm). Which revision is best?
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Quantify deviation. By Day 6, the Low Nutrient group (9.2 cm) is significantly below the predicted 12.0 cm (6 days * 2.0 cm/day). The High Nutrient group remains near the prediction. Step 2: Link to condition. The slowdown is specific to the Low Nutrient treatment and begins after Day 4. Step 3: Revise minimally. The best revision adds a nutrient-dependent slowdown: high nutrients sustain ~2.0 cm/day, while low nutrients cause the rate to drop after Day 4. This explains the data and allows for testing nutrient concentrations in future trials.

common_mistakes: Attributing systematic, repeating deviations to 'measurement error' when a clear pattern exists.
Choosing a revision that changes the model for all groups when the data only shows a change in one specific group.
Selecting a 'total overhaul' revision (like changing the fundamental shape of a graph) when a minor adjustment to a single variable is sufficient.
exam_tips: Look for the 'break point' in the data—the specific value or time where the observations stop matching the model.
If two groups are treated differently and their results diverge, the correct revision must mention the variable that separates them.
Eliminate answer choices that suggest a model is 'perfect' if the data shows a consistent gap larger than 5-10%.
content.recap: To revise a model, identify the consistent gap between prediction and data, link that gap to a specific experimental variable, and choose the smallest possible adjustment that accounts for the new evidence while remaining testable.

knowledge_claims.content: A model revision is necessary when observed data show a consistent deviation from predicted values that exceeds expected measurement noise.
The first step in revising a model is to quantify the magnitude and starting point of the gap between predictions and observations.
Condition linkage is the process of identifying which specific experimental variable or condition correlates with a model's failure to predict outcomes.
When updating a model, the principle of minimal revision dictates choosing the smallest change that explains the new data pattern.
A valid revised model must be able to generate a new, testable prediction that can be verified through further experimentation.
It is a mistake to attribute a repeating, systematic divergence in data to random measurement error.
If a model's predictions hold true for one experimental group but fail for another, the revision must incorporate the variable that distinguishes those two groups.
A minimal revision is preferred over a total model overhaul if the original model still accurately predicts behavior for some conditions or timeframes.
If data shows a growth rate slowing down only after a certain time, the revised model should include a time-dependent rate change rather than a new constant rate for the whole duration.
A 'signal' for revision is identified by a pattern of deviation that repeats under the same experimental conditions.
To verify a revision, use the updated model to calculate a predicted value for a new observation and check if it matches experimental results.
Covariation occurs when the magnitude of the deviation from a model changes in direct relation to the intensity or level of an experimental variable.

items.stem:
SCIENCE MATERIAL SET 1
Students tested how water temperature affected the time required for a tablet to dissolve. They used identical tablets, 100 mL of water in each cup, and stirred each cup at the same rate.

TABLE 1
Temperature (°C) | Dissolving time (s)
10 | 29
20 | 21
30 | 16
40 | 12

Trial 2 repeated the procedure with twice the water volume. Researcher 1 claims that higher temperature increases particle motion and therefore decreases dissolving time. Researcher 2 agrees that temperature matters but claims that stirring rate is the dominant factor whenever stirring is not controlled.

If Trial 2 shows longer times at every temperature, the model should be revised to include:
A) cup color as the only factor
B) water volume as an additional factor
C) the claim that temperature has no values
D) a rule that ignores Trial 2

options.A: cup color as the only factor
options.B: water volume as an additional factor
options.C: the claim that temperature has no values

items.explanation: The keyed response follows the material and directly targets 依据证据修正预测或模型.

videoLesson.title: Revise Model Predictions Based On Evidence
videoLesson.description: Recognize where predictions diverge from data and which variables align with that change. Quantify the gap and minimally update the model to yield a new testable prediction.
